messages.text: What is this paper about and what did they find?

messages.short_answer: PromptScaffold is a prompt editor that guides non-expert users through a four-slot template (role, task, examples, output format) to write LLM prompts. In a 16-participant within-subjects lab study, template prompts scored higher on an automatic task score (0.74 vs. 0.61) and gave higher self-reported confidence, though they took slightly longer to write.

sections.title: What the paper proposes and tested
sections.text: The authors built PromptScaffold, which splits a prompt into role, task, examples and output format slots, each with a short hint and an example, and assembles them into one editable prompt. They compared it with free-form prompting in a within-subjects study on three predefined tasks (sentiment classification, topic labelling and news summarisation), with time to final prompt and confidence also recorded.

sections.title: Main findings and what they did not show
sections.text: Template prompts reached a higher task score on average, with the largest gap on topic labelling, which the authors link to participants adding labelled examples. The authors also report that the template did not teach participants why the slots matter, and that several filled the slots mechanically. According to the overview summary, the template took longer to complete (7.5 vs. 6.2 minutes).

Studies of prompt writing describe non-experts as relying on trial and error and on conversational phrasing. Prompt libraries and prompt-pattern catalogues offer reusable structures, but they are usually written for developers and have rarely been evaluated with non-expert users in a controlled setting. 3 The PromptScaffold Editor PromptScaffold splits a prompt into four slots. The role slot states who the model should act as. The task slot describes what to do, with a hint to name the input and the goal. The examples slot asks for one to three inputoutput pairs, and the output format slot asks how the answer should be structured. Each slot shows a short hint and an example. The editor assembles the slots into one prompt that the user can preview and edit freely before running it. Procedure and measures. Each session lasted about 70 minutes in our lab. The main outcome was an automatic task score between 0 and 1: accuracy against gold labels for the two classification tasks and a reference-based overlap score for summaries. After each condition, participants rated their confidence in their prompts on a 7-point scale. We also recorded the time to the final prompt and held a short interview at the end of the session. 5 Results Prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher task score than free-form prompts (Table 1). The difference was largest for the topic-labelling task, where the examples slot led most participants to add labelled examples.

People without training in machine learning increasingly write prompts for large language model (LLM) tools, but often struggle to state the task, give examples and specify the output format. We present PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides users through a structured template with four slots: role, task, examples and output format.
